myths: EventBridge is just a renamed CloudWatch Events — it began there but adds custom buses, partner sources, schemas and replay.

services.name: AWS Step Functions
services.purpose: coordinates multiple services into serverless workflows with visual state machines, retries and error handling
services.beginner: Draws a multi-step process as a flowchart and then actually runs it — do this, if it fails wait and retry, then do that. Without it, all that 'what if this step fails' logic gets tangled through your code. You can watch each run progress step by step, which makes faults obvious.
services.videoTitle: AWS Step Functions explained in 90 seconds | Amazon Web Services
useCases: orchestrate a multi-step order pipeline
add retry and catch logic without writing it in every function
facts: Standard workflows are durable for up to a year and are billed per state transition; Express workflows are cheaper for high-volume, short runs.
Step Functions can call over 200 AWS services directly, avoiding glue Lambda functions.
myths: Step Functions replaces Lambda — it orchestrates Lambda and other services; it does not run your business logic itself.

services.name: AWS AppSync
services.purpose: is a managed GraphQL service that combines multiple data sources behind one API, with real-time subscriptions
services.beginner: Gives an app one place to ask for exactly the data it wants, even when that data lives in several different systems. Handy for phone apps, which waste battery and time making many separate requests. It can also push live updates to everyone viewing at once.
services.videoTitle: AWS AppSync Introduction
useCases: give a mobile app one query endpoint over several tables and services
push live updates to connected clients
facts: AppSync resolvers can talk directly to DynamoDB, Aurora, OpenSearch, Lambda and HTTP endpoints.
myths: AppSync is API Gateway for GraphQL — API Gateway can front a GraphQL server, but AppSync adds resolvers, caching and subscriptions natively.
pricing: Per million query and mutation operations

services.name: Amazon MQ
services.purpose: runs managed Apache ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ brokers for applications that need standard messaging protocols
services.beginner: Runs traditional message brokers that older enterprise software expects to talk to. It exists mainly so existing applications can move to AWS without being rewritten. For brand new work, SQS and SNS are usually cheaper and scale further.
services.videoTitle: Amazon MQ Demo - AWS
useCases: migrate an existing JMS or AMQP application without rewriting it
facts: Amazon MQ exists mainly for migration: it speaks industry-standard protocols that SQS and SNS do not.
myths: Amazon MQ is the default choice for new AWS applications — for new work SQS/SNS/EventBridge scale better and cost less.

services.name: AWS Amplify
services.purpose: builds, deploys and hosts full-stack web and mobile front ends with a connected AWS back end
services.beginner: Builds and hosts the part of a website people actually see, wired up to AWS services behind it. Push your code and it publishes automatically, distributed worldwide. Aimed at getting a working site up quickly without assembling the pieces yourself.
services.videoTitle: AWS Amplify: Fastest, Easiest Way to Develop Mobile and Web Apps That Scale
useCases: host a React or Next.js site with CI/CD from a Git branch
wire a front end to Cognito, AppSync and S3 quickly
facts: Amplify Hosting builds from your Git repository on push and serves through a managed CDN.
myths: Amplify is only a hosting service — it also generates and manages back-end resources.

services.name: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
services.purpose: ingests and stores large real-time data streams for multiple consumers to read
services.beginner: A conveyor belt for data arriving continuously — every click, every sensor reading. Several different systems can read the same belt independently, and it keeps recent data so a system that fell over can catch up. Built for information arriving constantly rather than in nightly batches.
services.videoTitle: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Fundamentals
useCases: clickstream and telemetry ingestion
let several applications process the same stream independently
facts: Records stay in the stream for a retention period (24 hours by default, up to 365 days), so multiple consumers can replay them.
Throughput scales by shard in provisioned mode, or automatically in on-demand mode.
myths: Kinesis Data Streams delivers straight into S3 or Redshift — that is Firehose; Data Streams is a stream you read from.

services.name: Amazon Data Firehose
services.purpose: delivers streaming data to destinations such as S3, Redshift, OpenSearch and Splunk with no code
services.beginner: Takes a continuous stream of incoming data and reliably drops it into storage, with no code to write. It gathers records for a few seconds or until it has enough, then delivers them in a batch. Simpler than a stream you read from, but only one destination and not instant.
services.videoTitle: Introduction to Kinesis Data Firehose | Amazon Web Services
useCases: land raw event data in S3 in near real time
buffer, compress and convert records on the way to storage
facts: Firehose is fully managed and near real time — it buffers by size or time before delivering, so it is not sub-second.
myths: Firehose lets several consumers read the same records — it is a delivery pipeline to a destination, not a replayable stream.

services.name: Amazon MSK
services.purpose: runs fully managed Apache Kafka clusters
services.beginner: Runs Apache Kafka, a widely used tool for moving large volumes of events between systems, without you maintaining the cluster. Because it is genuine Kafka, all the tools and code your team already has continue to work.
services.videoTitle: Get Started with Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK) | Amazon Web Services
useCases: move an existing Kafka workload to AWS unchanged
high-throughput event streaming with the Kafka ecosystem
facts: MSK runs real open-source Kafka, so existing Kafka clients, connectors and tooling work as-is.
myths: MSK is Kinesis with a different name — it is genuine Apache Kafka with its own APIs and operational model.

services.name: Amazon Athena
services.purpose: runs standard SQL directly against data in S3 with no infrastructure to manage
services.beginner: Lets you ask questions of files sitting in storage using ordinary database language, with no database to set up first. Point it at your files and start querying. You pay per amount of data it reads, so how you organise those files has a dramatic effect on the bill.
useCases: query log or CUR data in place
ad-hoc analysis of a data lake without loading a warehouse
facts: Athena charges per terabyte of data scanned, so partitioning and columnar formats such as Parquet cut cost dramatically.
Athena uses the AWS Glue Data Catalog for table definitions.
myths: Athena copies your data into a database first — it reads directly from S3.

services.name: AWS Glue
services.purpose: is a serverless data integration service providing a data catalog, crawlers and ETL jobs
services.beginner: The plumbing between data sources: it inspects your files to work out what is in them, keeps a catalogue of what lives where, and reshapes messy data into something tidy. Most analytics work is this unglamorous preparation, and the catalogue is used by several other AWS services.
services.videoTitle: What is AWS Glue?
useCases: crawl S3 and infer table schemas
transform raw data into partitioned Parquet for querying
facts: The Glue Data Catalog is a shared metadata store used by Athena, EMR, Redshift Spectrum and Lake Formation.
myths: Glue is only an ETL runner — its catalog is arguably its most widely used component.
pricing: Per DPU-hour for jobs and crawlers

services.name: Amazon EMR
services.purpose: runs big-data frameworks such as Spark, Hive and Presto on managed clusters
services.beginner: Rents you a cluster of machines running the standard big-data tools for processing enormous datasets in parallel. Where one computer would take a week, fifty computers take an afternoon. It can use cheap interruptible capacity, which cuts the cost sharply.
services.videoTitle: An introduction to Amazon EMR - Amazon Web Services
useCases: large-scale Spark transformations
existing Hadoop workloads moved to AWS
facts: EMR clusters can run task nodes on Spot Instances, which is a major cost lever for tolerant batch work.
myths: EMR is serverless by default — EMR Serverless exists, but classic EMR provisions a real cluster you size.
pricing: EC2 or EKS capacity plus an EMR per-instance surcharge

services.name: AWS Lake Formation
services.purpose: builds and secures a data lake with fine-grained permissions down to table, column and row level
services.beginner: Controls exactly who can see which parts of a large shared collection of data — right down to individual columns and rows. An analyst might see sales figures but not the customer names beside them. The data stays where it is; this governs access to it.
useCases: grant analysts access to some columns but not others
centralise data-lake permissions across accounts
facts: Lake Formation permissions are enforced by the query engines (Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR) that read the catalog.
myths: Lake Formation stores your data — the data stays in S3; Lake Formation governs access to it.
pricing: No charge for permissions; underlying services charged

services.name: Amazon OpenSearch Service
services.purpose: runs managed OpenSearch clusters for search, log analytics and vector similarity queries
services.beginner: A search engine you can point at your own data, whether that is a product catalogue or a mountain of log files. It is what makes searching for 'blue running shoes' return sensible results rather than exact matches only. It also stores data in the form modern AI applications need for finding relevant documents.
services.videoTitle: Amazon OpenSearch Service | Amazon Web Services
useCases: full-text search over a product catalogue
centralised log analytics with dashboards
vector store for retrieval-augmented generation
facts: OpenSearch supports k-nearest-neighbour vector search, which is why it appears in generative-AI reference architectures.
myths: OpenSearch is a relational database — it is a search and analytics engine with a different consistency and query model.

services.name: Amazon QuickSight
services.purpose: is a serverless business-intelligence service for dashboards and visualisations
services.beginner: Turns data into charts and dashboards that non-technical people can read, without them writing a single query. It keeps a fast copy of the data in memory so dashboards load quickly rather than hammering the source every time someone opens one.
services.videoTitle: Introducing Amazon QuickSight
useCases: publish dashboards over Redshift, Athena or S3 data
embed analytics in an application
facts: The SPICE in-memory engine caches data so dashboards stay fast without hitting the source on every view.
myths: QuickSight requires a data warehouse — it can query S3 through Athena, or several other sources directly.
pricing: Per author and per reader per month

services.name: Amazon SageMaker AI
services.purpose: covers the full machine-learning lifecycle: prepare data, train, tune, deploy and monitor models
services.beginner: The full workshop for building your own machine-learning model: prepare the data, train the model, test it, and put it live. This is the build-it-yourself option, for when no off-the-shelf model does what you need. Watch the cost — a model left running costs money whether anyone uses it or not.
services.videoTitle: Introduction to SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
useCases: train a custom model on your own data
host a real-time inference endpoint
run automated ML pipelines
facts: SageMaker is the build-your-own-model service; Bedrock is the use-someone-else's-foundation-model service.
Real-time endpoints bill for the instance while it exists, so idle endpoints are a common source of waste.
myths: SageMaker is a single tool — it is a family of capabilities (Studio, Training, Endpoints, Pipelines, Feature Store and more).

services.name: Amazon Bedrock
services.purpose: gives API access to foundation models from several providers, plus knowledge bases, agents and guardrails
services.beginner: Gives you access to powerful ready-made AI models through a simple request, without owning any of the machinery. Ask it to summarise a document or answer a question and it responds. It also provides safety filters and a way to ground answers in your own documents rather than general knowledge.
services.videoTitle: Introducing Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
useCases: add text generation or summarisation to an application
build retrieval-augmented generation over your own documents
facts: Bedrock is serverless — there is no model infrastructure to provision for on-demand inference.
Guardrails apply content filters and topic restrictions independently of which model you use.
Knowledge Bases handle the chunking, embedding and retrieval steps of a RAG pipeline for you.
myths: Bedrock trains models on your prompts — AWS states customer prompts and outputs are not used to train the base models.

services.name: Amazon Rekognition
services.purpose: analyses images and video for objects, scenes, text, faces and unsafe content
services.beginner: Looks at pictures and video and tells you what is in them — objects, text, faces, or content that breaks your rules. It works straight away with no training required. Commonly used to check user-uploaded photos automatically instead of having people review every one.
services.videoTitle: What Is Amazon Rekognition?
useCases: moderate user-uploaded images
detect and index faces in a media library
facts: Rekognition is a pre-trained API — you call it without training a model, though Custom Labels allows your own classes.
myths: Rekognition needs training data before it works — the standard APIs are pre-trained.
pricing: Per image or per minute of video analysed

services.name: Amazon Comprehend
services.purpose: extracts meaning from text: entities, key phrases, sentiment, language and PII
services.beginner: Reads text and pulls meaning out of it: the mood, the names mentioned, the main topics, and any personal information that should be hidden. Useful for sorting thousands of customer messages, or for stripping private details out of documents before sharing them.
services.videoTitle: What is Amazon Comprehend?
useCases: score support tickets for sentiment
redact personal data from documents
facts: Comprehend can detect and redact personally identifiable information, which is often used as a compliance control.
myths: Comprehend translates text — that is Amazon Translate.

services.name: Amazon Textract
services.purpose: extracts text, forms and tables from scanned documents
services.beginner: Reads scanned documents and pulls out the actual information, not just the words. It understands that a form has fields and a table has rows and columns, so an invoice comes back as structured data rather than a wall of text. That is the difference between this and basic text scanning.
services.videoTitle: What is Amazon Textract?
useCases: digitise invoices and claim forms
pull structured key-value pairs from PDFs
facts: Textract preserves structure — forms and tables come back as related fields, not one flat blob of text.
myths: Textract is plain OCR — it also understands form and table structure.

services.name: Amazon Transcribe
services.purpose: converts speech in audio and video into text
services.beginner: Turns spoken audio into written text. It can tell different speakers apart and be taught unusual words specific to your industry. Used for subtitles, meeting notes, and making recorded calls searchable.
services.videoTitle: What is Amazon Transcribe?
useCases: subtitle recorded media
transcribe and analyse contact-centre calls
facts: Transcribe supports speaker identification and custom vocabularies for domain-specific terms.
myths: Transcribe reads text aloud — that is Amazon Polly, the opposite direction.

services.name: Amazon Polly
services.purpose: turns text into lifelike speech
services.beginner: Turns written text into natural-sounding speech. Useful for reading articles aloud, voice responses, or accessibility. It is the opposite of Transcribe, which converts speech into text.
services.videoTitle: Text-to-Speech with Amazon Polly
useCases: voice responses in an application
audio versions of written articles
facts: Polly can return speech marks describing word timing, which is used to synchronise captions or animation.
myths: Polly transcribes speech — that is Amazon Transcribe.

services.name: Amazon Translate
services.purpose: performs neural machine translation between languages
services.beginner: Translates text between languages automatically. You can force particular translations for brand and product names so they are not mangled. Handy for supporting customers in languages your staff do not speak.
services.videoTitle: What is Amazon Translate?
useCases: localise user-generated content
translate support conversations in real time
facts: Custom terminology lets you force specific translations for brand and product names.
myths: Translate detects sentiment — that is Amazon Comprehend.

services.name: Amazon Lex
services.purpose: builds conversational interfaces — chatbots and voice bots — using intents and slots
services.beginner: Builds chatbots and voice assistants that recognise what someone wants and collect the details needed to act. It uses the same underlying technology as Alexa. It works from a defined set of intentions rather than free-form conversation.
services.videoTitle: Amazon Lex - Quickly Build Conversational Interfaces
useCases: automate common contact-centre questions
add a chat assistant to an application
facts: Lex uses the same automatic speech recognition and natural language understanding technology as Alexa.
myths: Lex is a foundation-model chatbot — it is intent-and-slot based; for open-ended generation use Bedrock.

services.name: Amazon Kendra
services.purpose: provides intelligent enterprise search across your document repositories using natural language
services.beginner: Search across all your company's scattered documents using ordinary questions rather than keywords. Ask 'how much holiday do I get?' and it finds the passage that answers it, wherever that document lives. Often used to give an AI assistant accurate, company-specific information.
services.videoTitle: What is Amazon Kendra?
useCases: search across SharePoint, S3 and Confluence from one place
retrieve context for a generative-AI answer
facts: Kendra returns ranked passages and direct answers, which makes it a common retrieval source in RAG architectures.
myths: Kendra is a keyword search index — it interprets natural-language questions rather than matching terms.

services.name: Amazon Q
services.purpose: is a generative-AI assistant that answers questions over your business data and helps developers write and update code
services.beginner: An AI assistant that answers questions using your own company's information, and helps developers understand and write code. Unlike a general chatbot it is connected to your systems, so its answers are about your business rather than the world at large.
useCases: answer staff questions grounded in internal documents
explain or refactor code in an IDE
facts: Amazon Q comes in variants aimed at business users and at developers, with different data connectors.
myths: Amazon Q is the same product as Bedrock — Bedrock is the model platform you build on; Q is a finished assistant.
pricing: Per user per month by edition

services.name: AWS CodePipeline
services.purpose: models and runs continuous delivery pipelines as a sequence of stages and actions
services.beginner: An assembly line for getting code from a developer's laptop into production. Each stage happens in order — build it, test it, ask a human to approve it, release it — and it runs automatically whenever code changes. It coordinates the stages; other tools do the actual work.
services.videoTitle: Introduction to AWS CodePipeline - Continuous Delivery on Amazon Web Services
useCases: build, test and deploy on every commit
add a manual approval gate before production
facts: CodePipeline orchestrates; the actual build and deploy work is done by CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, CloudFormation or third-party actions.
myths: CodePipeline compiles your code — CodeBuild does that.
pricing: Per active pipeline per month, or per action execution

services.name: AWS CodeBuild
services.purpose: compiles source, runs tests and produces deployable artifacts on managed build servers
services.beginner: Takes your code and turns it into something runnable, running the automated tests along the way. You pay per minute of building, so there is no idle machine sitting there costing money between releases.
services.videoTitle: AWS CodeBuild Overview
useCases: run unit tests on every pull request
build container images and push them to ECR
facts: CodeBuild bills per build minute by compute type, so there is no idle build fleet to pay for.
myths: CodeBuild deploys your application — deployment is CodeDeploy's or CloudFormation's job.
pricing: Per build minute by compute type

services.name: AWS CodeDeploy
services.purpose: automates application deployments to EC2, on-premises servers, Lambda and ECS with controlled rollout strategies
services.beginner: Handles the risky moment of putting new code onto live servers. It can release to a few users first, watch for errors, and roll back automatically if something goes wrong. That controlled release is what stops one bad change taking down everything.
services.videoTitle: Introduction to AWS CodeDeploy - Automated Software Deployment with Amazon Web Services
useCases: blue/green deployment with automatic rollback on alarm
canary shift of Lambda traffic
facts: CodeDeploy supports in-place, blue/green, canary and linear traffic-shifting strategies with automatic rollback.
myths: CodeDeploy only works on EC2 — it also deploys to Lambda, ECS and on-premises servers.
pricing: Free to EC2/Lambda/ECS; per on-premises instance update

services.name: AWS X-Ray
services.purpose: traces requests as they travel through a distributed application, showing where latency and errors occur
services.beginner: Follows a single request through every part of your system and shows exactly where the time went. When a page is slow and a dozen services were involved, this points at the guilty one. Ordinary monitoring shows overall averages; this shows individual journeys.
services.videoTitle: Optimize Application Performance with AWS X-Ray
useCases: find which microservice is slow in a chain of calls
visualise a service map of dependencies
facts: X-Ray shows per-request traces across services, which aggregate CloudWatch metrics cannot.
myths: X-Ray replaces CloudWatch Logs — it complements them with request-level tracing.

services.name: AWS CLI
services.purpose: is the command-line tool for controlling AWS services and scripting operations
services.beginner: Lets you control AWS by typing commands instead of clicking. Once a task needs doing repeatedly, a command can be saved and re-run reliably, which a human clicking through screens cannot match. It uses the same permissions as the website.
services.videoTitle: AWS Access Keys, CLI and SDK Introduction
useCases: script repeatable operational tasks
manage resources from a terminal or CI job
facts: The CLI uses the same public APIs and the same IAM permissions as the console.
myths: The CLI can do less than the console — it typically exposes new API capability before the console does.

services.name: AWS SDKs
services.purpose: are the language-specific libraries that let your application code call AWS APIs
services.beginner: Libraries that let your application code talk to AWS directly. They handle the fiddly, easy-to-get-wrong parts — proving who you are, retrying when the network hiccups — so you do not write that yourself. Notably, code running on AWS can use them without any password stored anywhere.
services.videoTitle: Getting Started with SDKs
useCases: call S3 or DynamoDB from application code
handle retries, signing and pagination correctly
facts: SDKs implement request signing, retries with backoff and credential resolution so you do not hand-roll them.
myths: You must embed access keys to use an SDK — on AWS compute the SDK picks up role credentials automatically.

services.name: AWS Migration Hub
services.purpose: tracks the progress of application migrations across AWS and partner migration tools in one place
services.beginner: A single progress board for a large move into AWS, pulling together status from whichever tools are doing the actual work. When hundreds of systems are moving, someone needs to know what is done. It tracks the move; it does not perform it.
services.videoTitle: Introducing AWS Migration Hub
useCases: report migration status to stakeholders
group servers into applications and follow their move
facts: Migration Hub aggregates status from tools such as Application Migration Service and DMS rather than moving data itself.
myths: Migration Hub performs the migration — it tracks migrations performed by other tools.

services.name: AWS Application Migration Service
services.purpose: lifts and shifts physical, virtual and cloud servers onto EC2 with continuous block-level replication
services.beginner: Copies entire existing servers into AWS while they keep running normally. It continuously mirrors changes, so when you finally switch over, only the last few minutes need catching up — minutes of downtime instead of a whole weekend. It moves things as they are; improving them comes later.
services.videoTitle: Introduction to AWS Application Migration Service | Amazon Web Services
useCases: rehost a data centre onto EC2 with minimal downtime
test a cutover without disrupting the source
facts: Continuous replication means cutover downtime is measured in minutes rather than the length of a full copy.
myths: It refactors applications for the cloud — it rehosts them as-is; modernisation is a separate exercise.
pricing: Per replicating source server per hour, with a free period

concepts.name: Regions and Availability Zones
concepts.purpose: describes how AWS divides the world into Regions, each containing multiple isolated Availability Zones
concepts.beginner: AWS has data centres all over the world, grouped into regions — London, Frankfurt, Virginia. Each region contains several separate sites with their own power and internet, close enough to work together but far enough apart that one flood or fire cannot take out both. Spreading across at least two is the basic recipe for staying online.
facts: An Availability Zone is one or more discrete data centres with independent power, cooling and networking.
Availability Zones within a Region are close enough for synchronous replication but far enough apart to fail independently.
Deploying across at least two Availability Zones is the baseline for high availability inside one Region.
myths: An Availability Zone is a single data centre — it is one or more.
Data is copied between Regions automatically — cross-Region replication is always something you configure.

concepts.name: Edge locations
concepts.purpose: are the global points of presence used to cache content and terminate connections close to users
concepts.beginner: Hundreds of small outposts spread far more widely than the main regions, used to hold copies of content close to users. They exist to shorten the distance data has to travel. You cannot run your own servers in them — they serve specific AWS services only.
facts: Edge locations serve CloudFront, Route 53, Global Accelerator, WAF and Shield, and vastly outnumber Regions.
myths: You launch EC2 instances in edge locations — you do not; edge locations run AWS edge services.

concepts.name: Shared responsibility model
concepts.purpose: divides security duties: AWS secures the cloud itself, you secure what you put in it
concepts.beginner: A clear split of the security work. AWS secures the building, the hardware and the underlying software; you secure what you put on top — your data, who has access, and how it is configured. Think of renting a flat: the landlord maintains the building and locks, but if you leave your own door open, that is on you.
facts: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud: hardware, the global infrastructure, and the managed service software.
You are responsible for security IN the cloud: your data, identity and access, OS patching where applicable, and network configuration.
The boundary moves with the service — with Lambda you never patch an OS, with EC2 you always do.
myths: AWS encrypts all your data automatically — you choose and configure encryption for most services.
Moving to managed services removes all your security duties — IAM, data classification and access control stay yours in every service.

concepts.name: AWS Well-Architected Framework pillars
concepts.purpose: gives six pillars for evaluating an architecture
concepts.beginner: AWS's checklist for judging whether a system is well built, covering six angles: running it smoothly, security, staying up, performing well, not wasting money, and environmental impact. It gives teams a shared vocabulary for the trade-offs they are already making. Note there are six — sustainability was added later, so older material lists five.
facts: The six pillars are Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization and Sustainability.
Sustainability was added as the sixth pillar in 2021.
myths: There are five pillars — Sustainability made it six.

concepts.name: Advantages of cloud computing
concepts.purpose: are the benefits AWS cites for moving from owned data centres to cloud
concepts.beginner: The core argument for renting computing rather than buying it: you pay only for what you use, you can start in minutes instead of months, and you can hand back capacity you no longer need. Because AWS buys hardware at enormous scale, its per-unit costs are lower than almost any single company could achieve. It is not automatically cheaper — it changes what you pay for and when.
facts: Trading capital expense for variable expense means you pay only for what you consume.
Massive economies of scale mean AWS's aggregate buying power produces lower per-unit prices than any one customer could reach.
You stop guessing capacity, gain speed and agility, stop spending money running data centres, and go global in minutes.
myths: Cloud is always cheaper than on-premises — it changes the cost model; steady predictable workloads can be cheaper owned.

concepts.name: Cloud deployment models
concepts.purpose: describes whether a workload runs entirely in the cloud, entirely on-premises, or across both
concepts.beginner: Three ways of arranging things: everything in the cloud, everything in your own building, or a mix of the two. The mixed approach is extremely common, usually because some systems are too old, too sensitive or too expensive to move. The two halves get joined by a private connection.
facts: The three models are cloud-based, on-premises (private cloud), and hybrid, which combines the two.
myths: Hybrid means running two separate systems — it means connecting them, typically with Direct Connect or VPN.

concepts.name: The migration strategies (the 7 Rs)
concepts.purpose: names the standard options for what to do with each application when moving to AWS
concepts.beginner: The standard menu of options for each application when moving to the cloud: move it as-is, tweak it slightly, rebuild it properly, replace it with something bought, switch it off, leave it where it is, or relocate it. Most large moves use several of these at once. Deciding which applies to what is most of the planning work.
facts: The seven are rehost, replatform, refactor, repurchase, retire, retain and relocate.
myths: Rehost and replatform are the same — rehost lifts the server as-is, replatform makes small optimisations such as moving to RDS.

concepts.name: EC2 purchasing options
concepts.purpose: are the ways you can pay for EC2 capacity, each trading flexibility for discount
concepts.beginner: Several ways to pay for the same computer. Pay as you go costs the most but you can stop any time; commit to a year or three and the price drops sharply; take spare capacity that can be taken back at two minutes' notice and it is cheaper still. It is the difference between a hotel, a lease and a last-minute cancellation deal.
facts: On-Demand has no commitment and the highest per-hour rate; it suits unpredictable or short workloads.
Reserved Instances and Savings Plans give large discounts for a one- or three-year commitment.
Spot Instances offer the deepest discount but can be interrupted with two minutes' notice.
Dedicated Hosts give you a physical server, which is usually about licensing compliance rather than performance.
myths: Spot Instances are cheaper Reserved Instances — Spot is interruptible spare capacity with no commitment or guarantee.
A Savings Plan locks you to one instance type — Compute Savings Plans apply across instance families, Regions, Lambda and Fargate.

concepts.name: AWS Support plans
concepts.purpose: are the tiers of technical support AWS sells, differing in response time and included services
concepts.beginner: Tiers of help you can buy, from free account and billing questions up to a named engineer who knows your business. The free level does not include help with technical problems, which surprises people. Higher tiers also unlock the full set of automated account checks.
concepts.videoTitle: AWS Support Overview | Amazon Web Services
facts: The tiers are Basic, Developer, Business, Enterprise On-Ramp and Enterprise.
A Technical Account Manager is included with Enterprise On-Ramp (pooled) and Enterprise (designated), not with Business.
Business and above include 24/7 phone, chat and email access to Cloud Support Engineers, plus the full Trusted Advisor check set.
myths: Basic Support includes technical help with your architecture — Basic covers billing and account questions plus service health, not technical troubleshooting.
Developer Support gives you 24/7 phone support — it gives business-hours email access to Cloud Support Associates.

concepts.name: Security groups versus network ACLs
concepts.purpose: distinguishes the two VPC firewall layers that candidates most often confuse
concepts.beginner: Two layers of network filtering that beginners constantly mix up. One attaches to individual machines and remembers conversations, so a reply to something you allowed out is automatically allowed back in. The other guards a whole neighbourhood, has no memory, and needs both directions written out — but it can explicitly ban an address, which the first cannot.
concepts.videoTitle: How do I configure and manage Amazon VPC security groups and network ACLs?
facts: Security groups are stateful: allow traffic in and the response is automatically allowed out.
Network ACLs are stateless: you must write both the inbound and the outbound rule.
Security groups only support allow rules; network ACLs support both allow and deny rules.
myths: Security groups can explicitly deny an IP address — they cannot; use a network ACL or AWS WAF for that.
Network ACLs attach to instances — they attach to subnets.

concepts.name: Horizontal and vertical scaling
concepts.purpose: describes the two directions you can add capacity
concepts.beginner: Two ways to cope with more work: a bigger machine, or more machines. More machines is generally preferred in the cloud, because it can be done automatically while running and because the work survives one machine dying. A bigger machine means switching the current one off to resize it.
facts: Scaling out (horizontal) adds more instances; scaling up (vertical) makes one instance bigger.
Horizontal scaling is what gives both elasticity and fault tolerance, because the work survives one instance failing.
myths: Vertical scaling has no downtime on EC2 — changing instance type requires stopping the instance.

concepts.name: High availability, fault tolerance and disaster recovery
concepts.purpose: separates three commonly conflated resilience goals
concepts.beginner: Staying up through everyday failures is a different problem from recovering after a disaster. The first spreads across nearby sites so one failure goes unnoticed; the second prepares for losing a whole region. Two numbers drive the design: how much data you can afford to lose, and how long you can afford to be down.
facts: High availability minimises downtime, usually across Availability Zones; disaster recovery restores service after a larger failure, usually across Regions.
RPO is how much data you can afford to lose; RTO is how long you can afford to be down.
The four common DR strategies, from cheapest and slowest to most expensive and fastest, are backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active/active.
myths: Multi-AZ is a disaster recovery strategy — it is high availability within one Region; DR normally implies a second Region.
Backups alone give you a low RTO — restoring large data sets takes time, which is exactly what pilot light and warm standby buy down.

concepts.name: Durability versus availability
concepts.purpose: separates the chance of losing data from the chance of not being able to reach it
concepts.beginner: Durability is whether your data still exists; availability is whether you can get at it right now. They are not the same — a file can be perfectly safe but temporarily unreachable. Storage options trade them off differently, which is why the cheaper tiers are worth reading carefully.
concepts.videoTitle: Amazon S3: Data Durability and Global Resiliency
facts: Durability is the probability an object survives; availability is the probability you can access it right now. S3 Standard quotes eleven nines of durability and four nines of availability.
myths: Higher durability implies higher availability — S3 One Zone-IA keeps the same durability design but lower availability.

concepts.name: Encryption at rest and in transit
concepts.purpose: distinguishes protecting stored data from protecting data moving over a network
concepts.beginner: Data needs protecting in two situations: sitting in storage, and travelling across a network. They are separate controls, and turning one on does not turn on the other. Scrambled data is useless to anyone without the key, which is why a stolen encrypted disk is far less serious than a stolen plain one.
facts: Encryption at rest protects stored data, typically with KMS keys; encryption in transit protects data on the wire, typically with TLS.
Server-side encryption is done by the AWS service; client-side encryption happens in your application before the data is sent.
myths: Enabling encryption at rest also encrypts traffic to the service — they are separate controls.

concepts.name: Least privilege and IAM best practice
concepts.purpose: is the principle of granting only the permissions a task actually needs
concepts.beginner: Give every person and program exactly the access they need for their job and nothing more. The point is damage limitation: if an account is compromised, the attacker inherits only what it could do. It is the single most repeated piece of security advice, and the most commonly ignored.
facts: Grant permissions to roles and groups rather than to individual users, and prefer temporary credentials over long-lived access keys.
Enable MFA on the root user, remove its access keys, and use it only for the few tasks that require it.
myths: Attaching AdministratorAccess to a role is fine if only a few people can assume it — least privilege applies to the role's permissions, not only to who can assume it.

concepts.name: Infrastructure as code
concepts.purpose: means defining infrastructure in version-controlled templates rather than clicking through a console
concepts.beginner: Writing down your setup as files kept alongside your code, rather than clicking through screens and hoping to remember. It means anyone can rebuild it identically, changes can be reviewed before they happen, and you have a record of why things are as they are.
facts: Infrastructure as code makes environments reproducible and changes reviewable, and is a core Operational Excellence practice.
myths: Infrastructure as code is only for large teams — reproducibility matters at any size.

concepts.name: Tagging and cost allocation
concepts.purpose: attaches key-value metadata to resources so they can be grouped for cost, automation and access control
concepts.beginner: Sticking labels on things — which team, which project, which environment. Without labels, a large bill is an unreadable list and nobody knows who owns what. Labels have to be switched on for billing before they show up in cost reports, and they do not apply to past bills.
facts: Cost allocation tags must be activated in the billing console before they appear in Cost Explorer and the Cost and Usage Report.
Tags can drive IAM conditions and automation as well as cost reporting.
myths: Tags apply retroactively to past bills — activated cost allocation tags only affect data from activation onwards.

concepts.name: Service quotas
concepts.purpose: are the per-account, per-Region limits AWS applies to resource counts and API rates
concepts.beginner: Built-in ceilings on how much of each thing one account can create. They exist to prevent runaway mistakes and runaway bills. Most can be raised by asking, but discovering one during a busy period is a bad time, so it is worth checking headroom in advance.
facts: Many quotas are soft and can be raised on request; some are hard limits that cannot be changed.
myths: Quotas are global — most are per-Region as well as per-account.

concepts.name: Loose coupling
concepts.purpose: means components communicate through a queue, topic or load balancer rather than calling each other directly
concepts.beginner: Letting parts of a system talk through a queue or a middleman rather than calling each other directly. If one part slows down or falls over, the rest keep working and the messages wait. The cost is a little added delay, bought in exchange for the whole thing not collapsing together.
facts: Decoupling with SQS or SNS lets one component fail or slow down without taking the rest of the system with it.
myths: Decoupling always improves latency — it improves resilience and scalability, often at the cost of added latency.

concepts.name: Stateless application design
concepts.purpose: keeps session data outside the application server so any instance can serve any request
concepts.beginner: Designing servers so none of them remembers anything important about a particular user, keeping that information in a shared store instead. Then any server can handle any request, and machines can be added or replaced freely. If a server remembers your shopping basket, losing that server loses the basket.
facts: Storing session state in DynamoDB or ElastiCache is what allows instances to be added and removed freely.
myths: Sticky sessions solve statelessness — they work around it and undermine even load distribution and instance replacement.

concepts.name: Caching strategy
concepts.purpose: stores frequently read data closer to the consumer to cut latency, load and cost
concepts.beginner: Keeping a copy of frequently requested things somewhere fast and close, rather than fetching them from source every time. It cuts waiting, load and cost at once. The hard part is knowing when the copy has gone stale, which is a genuinely difficult problem.
facts: Caching happens at several layers: CloudFront at the edge, ElastiCache in front of a database, and DAX in front of DynamoDB.
myths: Caching everything is always a win — stale data and cache invalidation costs are real design problems.

concepts.name: Capital versus operating expenditure
concepts.purpose: contrasts buying assets up front with paying for consumption
concepts.beginner: Buying servers means a large payment up front for equipment you then own and must replace. Renting means a smaller ongoing bill that rises and falls with what you use. Neither is automatically better, but they suit very different situations and appear quite differently in a company's accounts.
facts: Cloud converts up-front capital expenditure on hardware into variable operating expenditure billed on usage.
myths: Reserved Instances are a capital expense — they are still operating expense, just committed.

concepts.name: Total cost of ownership
concepts.purpose: accounts for every cost of running a workload, not just the visible server price
concepts.beginner: The honest total of what running something costs, not just the obvious price. An owned server costs its purchase price plus power, cooling, floor space, replacement every few years, and the salaries of the people maintaining it. Comparing a cloud bill against only the hardware price is the classic mistake.
concepts.videoTitle: Total Cost of Ownership of Cloud
facts: A fair on-premises comparison must include power, cooling, floor space, hardware refresh and the staff who run it.
myths: Comparing an EC2 bill to a server's purchase price is a valid TCO comparison — it ignores the majority of on-premises costs.
